before.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

before.label: Freudian psychoanalysis
before.description: A theory of mental life and a clinical practice that emphasizes unconscious conflict, childhood, sexuality, and interpretation. Its later historical uses vary. Freud provides a shared antecedent for psychoanalytic history and Lacan’s different reworking of subjectivity; neither branch represents every Freudian tradition.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Sigmund Freud; later adaptations include Erik Erikson’s historical psychobiography and Jacques Lacan’s rereading through language. Historical interpretation must address evidence and context rather than assume access to an unrecorded inner life.

representative_people.context: Psychoanalysis, a resource for different later projects.
Historical psychobiography.

before.scope_note: Clinical psychoanalysis, Lacan’s rereading, and historical psychobiography are separate uses; historical interpretation cannot assume access to unrecorded motives.

after.label: Freudian psychoanalysis
after.description: A clinical practice and family of theories concerning unconscious conflict, development, sexuality, interpretation and relationships. Freud’s changing methods, later child-analysis disputes, psychosocial history, linguistic rereading and feminist adaptations require distinct accounts.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Sigmund Freud; later adaptations include Erik Erikson’s historical psychobiography and Jacques Lacan’s rereading through language. Historical interpretation must address evidence and context rather than assume access to an unrecorded inner life.

representative_people.context: Develops an account of repression, association, dreams, sexuality and transference, then investigates group bonds. These are historically situated theoretical arguments; his clinical claims are not a substitute for evidence about people in the past.

after.scope_note: This is a tradition entry, not an individual Freud node. Clinical claims and normative sexual classifications are historically situated. Breuer treated Anna O.; Freud’s account is not an independent outcome audit. Klein, Anna Freud, Erikson, Lacan and feminist interpreters pursue divergent questions. Historical motive inference requires documentary criticism; neither clinical access nor a uniform Freudian school can be assumed. Primary readings here cover the Clark lectures and selected Group Psychology chapters, not Freud’s entire career.

strands.title: Catharsis, repression and changing methods
strands.focus: Freud distinguishes Breuer’s earlier practice, hypnotic experiments and his developing use of association. His retrospective narrative does not establish clinical outcomes.

strands.title: Association, dreams and indirect expression
strands.focus: Manifest and latent dream material, condensation, displacement and everyday errors form different routes in Freud’s interpretation. Psychic determination remains a theoretical premise to examine.

strands.title: Development, transference and sublimation
strands.focus: Freud’s sexuality extends beyond reproduction; transference and sublimation connect his developmental and clinical account. Its normative sexual classifications are historical judgments.

strands.title: Individual relations and group bonds
strands.focus: Group Psychology starts with relations already present in individual life and questions suggestion as a sufficient explanation, proposing libidinal attachments.

strands.title: Child analysis and divergent developments
strands.focus: Klein’s play interpretation differs from other early child-analysis practices. Anna Freud and Klein are not interchangeable extensions of Freud; support here is a retrospective institutional profile.

strands.title: Psychosocial and historical adaptations
strands.focus: Erikson examines identity in historical orders; Gay argues for a place within contextual history. Neither position represents all psychoanalytic traditions.

strands.title: Feminist questions and subjectivity

strands.title: Translation, context and historical inference
strands.focus: Schapiro’s Leonardo criticism tests an application against historical knowledge while retaining the possibility of psychological inquiry. Unrecorded motives are not directly accessible clinical facts.

before.label: Psychohistory / psychoanalytic history
before.description: Uses psychoanalytic ideas to investigate motivations, identity, childhood, and relationships in historical settings. Includes psychobiography and broader psychoanalytically informed history. Disputes concern evidentiary limits, retrospective interpretation, and reduction of political or social processes to individual psychology.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Erik H. Erikson, Young Man Luther: A Study in Psychoanalysis and History (1958); Peter Gay, Freud for Historians (1985). These projects should not be treated as straightforward applications of Lacan.

after.label: Psychohistory / psychoanalytic history
after.description: A contested range of historical uses of psychological interpretation: psychosocial life studies, psychoanalytically informed contextual history and theories of childrearing and collective fantasy. Disagreements concern sources, explanatory scale, historical variability and retrospective inference.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Erik H. Erikson, Young Man Luther: A Study in Psychoanalysis and History (1958); Peter Gay, Freud for Historians (1985). These projects should not be treated as straightforward applications of Lacan.

strands.title: Psychobiography and historical knowledge

strands.title: Historicizing psychological concepts
strands.focus: Erikson asks for historical scrutiny of identity crises and the categories used to describe them. Retrospective self-interpretation itself becomes evidence requiring criticism.

freud.people: Preserve Freud, Erikson and Lacan; add Breuer, Charcot, Bernheim, Jung and Ferenczi as dated clinical resources, Anna Freud and Klein as divergent later contributors, Mitchell as a feminist interpreter and Schapiro as a critic. Thirteen new shared identities across the batch; no new full nodes. Breuer treated Anna O.; Freud did not. Clinical analysts and historians retain distinct contextual roles.
freud.works_and_arguments: Read all five Clark lectures and their notes, plus Group Psychology I/IV and translator note. Fill Freud’s blank with actual primary works, distinguishing 1909 lectures/1910 publication and 1921 German/1922 English. Repression, association, dream-work, broad sexuality, transference and group bonds gain contextual explanation. Original German witnesses, Freud’s later revisions and clinical outcomes are not independently verified.
freud.internal_distinctions: Eight approaches separate changing methods, indirect interpretation, development/transference, group relations, child-analysis differences, historical adaptations, feminist uses and historical inference limits. Klein support is a retrospective institutional profile, Mitchell a publisher description. Lacan’s existing scoped attribution remains, with a full individual review next; no invented unified psychoanalytic school.
freud.incoming_connections: Schapiro supplies a specific critical exchange concerning Freud’s Leonardo interpretation. Clinical antecedents are explicit within the roster and methods, without fabricated full-node arrows. Freud’s own account credits collaborators and earlier experiments; it is not a neutral adjudication of origins. His 1917 origin narrative was partly researched but not added to the graph.
freud.outgoing_connections: Clarify differentiated Erikson/Gay/deMause contributions and give the Frankfurt link a named Neumann/Marcuse reading setting from Gay’s recollection. Preserve existing primary Fanon sociogeny qualification and Alexander Workshop link. Lacan influence stays distinct from psychohistory; Elias remains undirected affinity without invented borrowing. Named reception is not general endorsement.
freud.evidence_and_interpretation: Source notes distinguish full lecture reading, selected chapters, primary retrospectives, criticism and publisher/institutional summaries. Freud’s clinical success claims, normative sexual classifications and interpretations of opponents are attributed, not established facts. Schapiro’s translation/context objections do not disprove all psychoanalysis. Original works by later clinical contributors remain concrete follow-ups.

psychohistory.people: Expand Erikson/Gay with deMause, Demos, Schapiro, Pollock and the Neumann/Marcuse resource circle. Distinguish practitioners, methodological critics and contributors rather than assigning blanket membership. The selection improves key methodological disagreements but does not exhaust political, religious or non-European psychohistory.
psychohistory.works_and_arguments: Read Gay’s complete available 1997 interview, deMause’s complete 1982 preface and bounded 1988 reply, Erikson’s 1970 primary selections, Schapiro’s selected 1956 criticism and Pollock’s complete thesis section 2.2.3. Erikson’s own p. 750 explains his Luther interpretation, but it is not a newly read page from the 1958 book. Original case books and diary witnesses remain distinct from reception evidence.
psychohistory.internal_distinctions: Six approaches distinguish psychosocial lives, contextual psychoanalytic history, psychogenic causal theory, childhood evidence disputes, psychobiographical inference and historical scrutiny of concepts. Gay and deMause’s programs are editorially compared across texts, not represented as a personal exchange. deMause says modes can coexist; no universal modern happy ending or accepted group diagnosis is asserted.
psychohistory.incoming_connections: Add the specific Frankfurt reading-circle impetus to Gay and deMause’s explicit appropriation of Kuhn. Pollock’s 1981 thesis supplies a critical incoming childhood-history intervention. Kuhn’s endorsement is not claimed; treating opposition as a paradigm conflict does not validate deMause’s historical theory. The demography umbrella connection is specifically childhood/family history.
psychohistory.outgoing_connections: Clarify Erikson’s contribution to biography with his own later formulation, while preserving the comparison with social history as undirected. Add Schapiro’s methodological criticism of Freud and deMause’s criticism of Pollock’s 1983 book. Reciprocal childhood-history critiques concern different texts; no independent source collation or settled verdict is implied.
psychohistory.evidence_and_interpretation: Resolve the earlier Erikson primary-method follow-up with a documented limit: public book routes supplied metadata/borrowing access, while the 1970 authorial retrospective provides a bounded primary formulation. It does not upgrade the original book. Pollock thesis and later book stay distinct. deMause’s cultural stereotypes, clinical claims and claims about reception are not adopted. Further primary clinical/feminist and case evidence is bounded below.
